entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Alcibiades (c. 450 – 403 BCE) emerged as one of the most brilliant yet erratic figures of Classical Athens, a statesman and general whose ambitious policies and personal charisma profoundly impacted the Peloponnesian War. Born into the aristocratic Alcmaeonid family, a lineage linked to Cleisthenes and Pericles, he inherited immense wealth and political influence, positioning him at the heart of Athenian power struggles. His career unfolded across the Aegean and Ionian Seas, critically influencing the destinies of Athens, Sparta, and Persia during a period of intense geopolitical flux, ultimately contributing to the demise of Athenian naval hegemony.

His early political ascendancy saw him championing an aggressive expansionist foreign policy, most notably advocating for the disastrous Sicilian Expedition in 415 BCE. Despite initial strategic successes, accusations of sacrilege—the mutilation of the Hermai and parody of the Eleusinian Mysteries—forced his flight to Sparta, where he became a crucial advisor, revealing Athenian weaknesses and orchestrating the Spartan fortification of Decelea. Later, he defected to the Persian satrap Tissaphernes, manipulating both sides before being recalled by the Athenian fleet at Samos in 411 BCE. His subsequent victories at Cynossema (411 BCE), Abydos (410 BCE), and Cyzicus (410 BCE) temporarily restored Athenian naval supremacy and led to his triumphant return to Athens in 407 BCE.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Alcibiades's strategic brilliance and political opportunism significantly shaped the latter half of the Peloponnesian War, directly contributing to Athens's eventual defeat through his counsel to Sparta and the disastrous Sicilian Expedition.
